earlier_scan.source_named: Retired ISO entry, duplicate of Prai [prt]/phai1238. Filbeck, David. 1978. T'in: A Historical Study (Pacific Linguistics) covers Prai/T'in varieties and plausibly stress; not readable online. Wikipedia Prai phonology (Moran et al. PHOIBLE) has no stress statement

new_statements.quote: p. 91: "A syllable is said to be stressed if it is more prominent than the surrounding syllables. In Pray, stress is predictable. It is conditioned by the position of the syllable in the stress group, that is, stress always falls on the last syllable of a stress group." p. 28: "The stress group in Pray may have from one to three syllables, but the majority is monosyllabic. If it has two or more syllables, it has as its nucleus one stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group." p. 34: "A minor syllable functions as a periphery in the stress group. Its occurrence is optional. It bears no stress, and normally occupies the initial position of the stress group, preceding the major syllable."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Prai (Pray) words are 'stress groups' of one to three syllables: an obligatory final major syllable optionally preceded by one (rarely two) short-vowel minor syllables (e.g. /si-/, /ka-/, /pa-/). Stress is non-contrastive and always on the last syllable, i.e. the major syllable ([si'ne:] 'mouse', [ka'cay] 'horns', [si lap'phlap] 'butterfly'); minor syllables are never stressed. Pitch is also predictable from syllable shape (level vs high-falling), so Pray is not tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated for Pray; only stressed (major) vs unstressed (minor) syllables are distinguished, and pitch on a minor syllable is 'neutral' (p. 30). For the sister dialect Mal, Filbeck (1976: 248-250; summarised by Singnoi p. 93 and L-Thongkum & Intajamornrak 2008: 63) describes three sentence-level stress degrees and two word stresses.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the two trisyllabic words found ([si lap'phlap] 'butterfly', [si rak'thak] 'a kind of lizard') still stress the final major syllable; a minor syllable 'in rare cases' occurs medially (p. 34).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'stress group', the word-sized unit of one major syllable plus optional minor syllables, functioning inside the intonation group; 'there is no distinction between stress groups' by sentence position (sec. 2.2, p. 30). Elicited citation-form data from one main informant plus other speakers of Ban Wang Saw, Chiang Klang district, Nan.
new_statements.identity_note: pray1239 'Pray 3' [pry] is not a distinct language: ISO 639-3 CR 2015-045 (saved, p. 2) retired [pry] on 2016-01-15 as 'a dialect of Prai found at Ban Wen' and merged it into Prai [prt] = Glottolog phai1238 (family Austroasiatic, Khmuic; Glottolog now lists pray1239 under Bookkeeping with zero descriptive references). The stress statement quoted is Singnoi 1988's description of the Pray (Prai) of Ban Wang Saw, Chiang Klang district, Nan, i.e. phai1238, not specifically the Ban Wen village variety; Jordan-Diller 2004 (pp. 38-40) report that Prai speakers consider Ban Wen speech closer to Mal (mall1246). The same Singnoi statement is already staged as a new statement under phai1238 in webcat (world_status 'statement found in an open source'). Per the census counting law (retired codes confer no identity), pray1239 should be recorded as a pointer/duplicate of phai1238, not as a separate catalog entity.

sources.note: Sec. 4.3.2 'Stress', p. 91: stress in Pray is predictable and always falls on the last syllable of the stress group; sec. 2 'Stress Group', p. 28: stress groups are 1-3 syllables, nucleus = one stressed syllable, always the last; sec. 3.2.2, p. 34: minor syllables bear no stress and precede the major syllable. Pitch also predictable (pp. 89-91), so Pray is non-tonal. Verified on the page image of p. 91.

sources.citation: Filbeck, David. 1976. Mal (Thin). In William A. Smalley (ed.), Phonemes and orthography: language planning in ten minority languages of Thailand, 239-257. Pacific Linguistics C-43. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Describes Mal (mall1246), not Prai: three sentence stresses (1 heavy/high pitch, 2 medium/mid, 3 weak/low) forming the intonation contour, pp. 248-250; footnote p. 250: 'word stress (of which there are two) often coalesce with sentence stress'; primary/secondary stress pitch (falling vs level) depends on syllable shape. Not a Prai statement.
Bookkeeping entry: 'retired in ISO 639-3... duplicate of [prt] Prai', change request 2015-045, effective 2016-01-15; no descriptive references.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2015. Change Request 2015-045: retire [pry] Pray 3 (submitted by Nate Cheeseman, SIL, with J. & K. Diller and Theraphan L-Thongkum; adopted, effective 2016-01-15).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Identity record only: 'This is a variety that is fully intelligible with another ISO 639-3 language and should be merged with it... [prt] Prai. Rationale: Pray 3 is actually a dialect of Prai found at Ban Wen' (p. 2); sources cited: Jordan-Diller & Diller 2004 MKS 34 pp. 38, 40 and Filbeck 1978 (p. 4).

sources.citation: L-Thongkum, Theraphan & Chommanad Intajamornrak. 2008. Tonal evolution induced by language contact: a case study of the T'in (Lua') language of Nan province, northern Thailand. Mon-Khmer Studies 38: 57-68.
sources.note: On Pray: 'there are no consistent pitch patterns in Pray, even in the speech of a single speaker' (abstract p. 57, p. 66) - Pray is non-tonal while Bo Kluea Mal has acquired two tones. Stress is mentioned only in summarising Filbeck 1972 on Mal: 'The Mal variety which he studied comprises three degrees of stress and three types of pitch' (p. 63, Figure 2). No Pray stress rule.

sources.citation: Jordan-Diller, Kari & Jason Diller. 2004. The Prai of northern Thailand: a sociolinguistic survey of a Mon-Khmer language. Mon-Khmer Studies 34: 19-45.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Identity: pp. 38-40, Prai villagers report that 'Ban Wen village and those in the area speak more like the Mal people than the Prai people' and that Ban Wen is where Prai is spoken 'worst'; Ban Wen listed among Prai villages (p. 44).

sources.citation: Filbeck, David. 1978. T'in: a historical study. Pacific Linguistics B-49. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Passing statements only: p. 17, Thai and T'in dialects 'both contain bisyllabic word patterns of minor (stressless) syllable plus major (stressed) syllable'; p. 84 (transcription note) vowel length is only discernible in an identical 'stress position of a sentence', 'in a weak stress position (cf. Filbeck 1965: 46) a long vowel is likely to be measurably shorter than a short vowel in a stronger stress position'. Also p. 10: Baw Wen (Ban Wen) village T'in speakers are trilingual with Meo. No dedicated stress rule.
